narrative: The model estimates a 48% chance that you will leave your job. In practical terms, that is a near-even risk—almost one in two—and under the promotion rule used here it is high enough to deny a promotion for now. The strongest influence was your report that you have no other job opportunities. That signal actually pushed toward staying, since outside offers usually increase leaving risk. The next most important signal was your total experience of 6–10 years, which pushed toward leaving; this is above the most common group among employees predicted to stay, where 1–5 years is most typical. Your 1–5 years in the current organization was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward leaving, suggesting that your current stage of tenure is associated with movement risk. So even though the single strongest factor favoured staying, the combined experience and tenure signals, plus smaller factors, left the overall risk near the decision boundary. Before reconsidering promotion, the organization should discuss your career path, development, workload, pay and recognition, and clarify what would make promotion viable. You should also raise any concerns about growth, support and job fit, because denying promotion without a clear plan may itself increase the chance you decide to leave.
